As part of our medicinal chemistry campaign, we also identified a structurally similar negative control, compound 5, which lacks in-cell affinity for TTBK1 and TTBK2. TTBK2 is an effector of ciliogenesis, acting in concert with CEP164, CP110, and CEP83 to initiate the biogenesis of primary cilia. We demonstrate that compound 13 ablates TTBK2 autophosphorylation and significantly disrupts ciliogenesis in hTERT-RPE-1 cells, making it a powerful tool compound for ciliary studies.

item.title: Rethinking log P : Lipophilicity =̷ Hydrophobicity
item.description:
Abstract
LogP values have served as cutoffs for hit-, lead-, and drug-likeness as well as thresholds for toxicity and ADME decision-making and are often characterized as lipophilicity. When the properties of octanol and the experimental limitations of logP measurements are considered, it becomes clear that logP > 3 must be due to increased hydrophobicity and not lipophilicity. We propose that the partition coefficient between either octanol or water and “the thermodynamic ideal solution” is a useful reference to separately determine octanol solvation (lipophilicity) and aqueous solvation (hydrophilicity). We further propose that the ideal solubility of solids measures “autophilicity”. Aqueous solvation spans many orders of magnitude, yet octanol solvation is much narrower, and thus lipophilicity is nearly constant. Understanding which molecules are hydrophobic, rather than lipophilic, can be critical in interpreting affinity, PK, ADME, safety, and other behaviors of molecules necessitating these more nuanced definitions.

item.title: Ligand-Dependent Affinity but State-Dominated Efficacy in Structure-Based GPCR Pharmacology Prediction
item.description:
Abstract
High accuracy in structure-based prediction of G protein-coupled receptor (GPCR) efficacy may reflect the receptor state rather than ligand-specific information. We addressed these information sources using state rules, ligand-blind baselines, matched receptor-state contrasts, ligand permutation, and out-of-distribution (OOD) evaluation, with affinity prediction as a positive control. State rules and ligand-blind geometry achieved binary-efficacy-balanced accuracies of 0.844−0.910 and 0.777−0.870, respectively. Of 75 ligand-aware evaluations, 72 failed at least one prespecified ligand-sensitivity condition, and three lacked required evidence; none met all required criteria. Affinity pretraining gave no detectable efficacy benefit over matched random initialization. In contrast, ligand chemistry supported affinity prediction across 14,740 measured pairs, and all 12 primary affinity permutation comparisons deteriorated, although this advantage did not persist under scaffold, family, or combined OOD splits. Accuracy on endpoint structures therefore cannot alone establish ligand-specific efficacy learning; the findings do not set a general limit on such learning.

item.title: The Phenotypic Hit-to-Probe Challenge
item.description:
Abstract
Phenotypic drug discovery (PDD) fuels the clinical pipelines with first-in-class therapeutic modalities. Success rates depend on the quality of the assay models and can be hampered by resource-intensive processes of target and mode-of-action deconvolution. A critical part of this practice is generating focused sets of phenotypic probes to accelerate in vivo validation and to support target/concept tractability and translatability, raising the question of which phenotypic hit analogues to synthesize as high-quality chemical probes for a given campaign. Here, we outline recommendations and discuss criteria tailored to the specific demands of phenotypic probes. With examples of successful PDD programs, some of which have yielded approved first-in-class drugs, we illustrate common design principles. These underscore that phenotypic probes benefit from (a) availability of matched pairs of active/inactive stereoisomers, (b) ligand topology-guided optimization, and (c) exit vectors for ADME- and target deconvolution-driven acceleration of early in vivo proof-of-concept and advancement towards clinical candidates.

item.title: Discovery of Anti-apoptotic BAX Inhibitors
item.description:
Abstract
BAX is a critical regulator of the apoptosis cascade and its abnormal activation contributes to the development of disease including cardiovascular and neurodegenerative disorders. Therefore, BAX represents an attractive target for the pharmacological inhibition of pathological cell death. Based on a virtual screen, we identified and modified several EGFR kinase inhibitors with potential activity against BAX. Systematic modifications of the dacomitinib and gefitinib core structure were performed, allowing us to elucidate how structural modifications influence biological activity and leading to a comprehensive structure-activity relationship (SAR) on BAX inhibition. The developed series has favorable drug-like properties and improved BAX inhibitory activity in vitro, in cells, and in human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived brain organoids, with significantly reduced EGFR kinase activity. This series therefore represents a promising starting point for the development of improved and potentially therapeutic BAX inhibitors.

item.title: FDA Approval of Ensitrelvir: an Oral, Nonpeptidic, Noncovalent SARS-CoV-2 Main Protease Inhibitor for Household Postexposure Prophylaxis

item.title: FAP-Triggered In Situ Self-Assembly of HPQ in Tumors Empowers 131 I Internal Radiotherapy
item.description:
Abstract
Fibroblast activating protein (FAP) is specifically overexpressed in malignant tumors. The 2-(2′-hydroxyphenyl)-4(3H)-quinazolinone (HPQ) scaffold exhibits hydrophobicity, aggregation-induced emission (AIE). The responsive probes built on HPQ can undergo in situ activation and self-assembling precipitation, enabling prolonged retention in lesion sites. Herein, a FAP-cleavable Cbz-Gly-Pro-sequence was conjugated to the phenolic hydroxyl of HPQ via a self-immolative linker, with phenol/tyrosine moieties for 131I labeling through aliphatic linkers, affording LWH-1 and LWH-2. LWH-3 further incorporated a tetraphenylethylene moiety, a PEG6-triazole-PEG6 linker, and (D-Tyr)5-NH2. All precursors for radioiodination responded efficiently to FAP, releasing HPQ-OH to generate AIE and illuminating tumors for over 48 h. [131I]LWH-3 showed a 2.76-fold higher molar activity than [131I]LWH-2 and an in vivo half-life of 43.66 min. In PC12-FAP xenografts, [131I]LWH-3 achieved outstanding antitumor efficacy with favorable biosafety. Transcriptomic and metabolomic analyses revealed that internal radiotherapy attenuated tumor metabolic adaptability by modulating fatty acid metabolism-associated networks to impair proliferation.

item.title: HER2-Targeting Affibody Equipped with Albumin-Binding Small Molecules for Radiotheranostics
item.description:
Abstract
HER2-targeting affibody radioprobes are often limited by rapid systemic clearance and excessive renal accumulation. Herein, we develop a modular chemical strategy to optimize the pharmacokinetic properties of affibodies through conjugation of small-molecule albumin-binding motifs (ABMs). Enabled by our selective S-glycosylation approach, ABMs were introduced via a sugar-based linker, allowing systematic modulation of probe behavior. Evaluation of sugar-modified variants revealed that sugar structure plays a critical role in regulating in vivo distribution, with the GalNAc-modified probe [68Ga]Ga-5c exhibiting favorable tumor-to-background contrast in PET/CT imaging. Further incorporation of ABMs afforded GalNAc-IPBA-functionalized affibody [177Lu]Lu-10a, which achieved an 17-fold extension of circulation half-life, reduced renal accumulation, and maintained efficient tumor targeting. Therapeutically, [177Lu]Lu-10a induced 86.25% tumor growth inhibition with minimal systemic toxicity. This study provides a modular strategy for overcoming pharmacokinetic limitations of affibody-based radiotheranostics.

item.title: Medicinal Chemistry Strategies for Targeting RNA-Binding Proteins: Design, Optimization, and Therapeutic Potential
item.description:
Abstract
RNA-binding proteins (RBPs) are essential regulators of post-transcriptional gene expression whose disruption contributes broadly to tumor initiation, progression, and therapeutic resistance. Through their control of RNA splicing, stability, translation, and epitranscriptomic modification, these proteins orchestrate oncogenic networks that sustain hallmark cancer phenotypes. This central role has stimulated intensive efforts to develop small-molecule RBP inhibitors, yielding mechanistically diverse compounds against m6A pathway components and classical oncogenic RBPs with demonstrated efficacy in preclinical models. However, substantial challenges remain, including achieving high target selectivity, optimizing drug-like properties, and addressing adaptive resistance mechanisms. This article examines recent advances in RBP-targeted therapeutics, highlighting design strategies, structural mechanisms, and key obstacles on the path toward clinical application.

item.title: Discovery and Optimization of Anticancer Dibenzothiazepinones That Target the Ribosome Biogenesis Factor NVL
item.description:
Abstract
Using inducible forward genetics, we recently discovered a dibenzothiazepinone (1) with activity against cancer cells via inhibition of the ribosome biogenesis factor NVL (nuclear valosin-containing protein-like). Herein, we delineate a comprehensive structure−activity relationship (SAR) study that explores the structural space surrounding the dibenzothiazepinone scaffold. A series of 115 analogs were synthesized and evaluated for activity against the colorectal cancer cell line HCT116 and counter-screened against cells CRISPR engineered to express a compound-resistant mutation in NVL. Our initial medicinal chemistry-driven campaign focused on improving potency, metabolic stability, and in vivo exposure and clearance. A fluorescence polarization assay with recombinant human NVL established a correlation between NVL-binding and antiproliferative activity. Cryo-EM structures of human NVL with select inhibitors revealed a binding mode that is consistent with the SAR data. This study led to the in vivo analog 100 (MM927), which we reported to suppress tumor growth in vivo without detectable toxicity via targeting the NVL.

item.title: Structure-Guided Discovery of Orally Bioavailable Allosteric SLC6A19 Inhibitors that Promote Urinary Amino Acid Excretion In Vivo
item.description:
Abstract
SLC6A19 is a sodium-dependent transporter that mediates the absorption of neutral amino acids in the intestine and reabsorption of these amino acids in the kidney. Pharmacological inhibition of SLC6A19 may provide therapeutic benefit by normalizing plasma amino acid levels and potentially reducing renal tubular transport burden. Virtual screening against an allosteric binding pocket observed in the cryo-EM structure of SLC6A19/cinromide (1) identified compound 6 as a promising hit. The cryo-EM structure of SLC6A19/CB3 (2) revealed a second, partially overlapping pocket adjacent to the compound 6 binding site. Analogue design merging these two binding pockets followed by optimization led to compound 20, a potent, selective, and orally bioavailable allosteric SLC6A19 inhibitor. While compound 20 demonstrates an approximately 10-fold rightward potency shift against mouse SLC6A19, it retains good potency against non-human primate SLC6A19. Consistent with the SLC6A19 inhibition mechanism, oral dosing of 20 led to increased urinary amino acid excretion in a dose-dependent manner in human SLC6A19 knock-in mice and wild-type non-human primates.

item.title: Discovery of GTA182, a Novel CNS-Active Tricyclic Amide MTA-Cooperative PRMT5 Inhibitor for MTAP -Deleted Cancers
item.description:
Abstract
Developing central nervous system (CNS) active, MTA-cooperative PRMT5 inhibitors for MTAP-deleted malignancies represents a formidable challenge. Here, we report the discovery of GTA182 via structure-based drug design. Multi-parameter optimization balanced single-digit nanomolar potency and >100-fold MTAP-deletion selectivity with dose-proportional pharmacokinetics. Optimized physicochemical properties, and minimal efflux delivered unbound brain concentrations within the efficacious range. Oral GTA182 demonstrated robust MTAP deletion-dependent efficacy, achieving net regression at 30 mg/kg (102% TGI) in MTAP-deleted HCT116 xenografts (versus 41% TGI in WT) alongside 59% regression and extended median survival (>91 days) in the orthotopic U87MG-luc glioblastoma model. In a Phase I trial (CTR20243795), GTA182 was well tolerated, shrank intracranial tumors, and achieved an overall objective response rate (ORR) approaching 30%. These properties establish GTA182 as a promising therapeutic candidate for MTAP-deleted systemic and CNS malignancies.

item.title: Discovery of Tricyclic Oxazinoquinolinone-Based BCL6 PROTAC Degraders with Potent Activity Against Diffuse Large B-Cell Lymphoma
item.description:
Abstract
B-cell lymphoma 6 (BCL6) is a key transcriptional repressor involved in the pathogenesis of diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL). In this study, scaffold hopping of BI-3802 led to compound 1, a new tricyclic BCL6-targeting ligand. Further optimization of linker architecture and CRBN-recruiting motifs led to compound 15, a potent BCL6 PROTAC degrader, which induced rapid and efficient BCL6 degradation in OCI-LY1 cells (DC50 = 5.32 nM) and displayed potent antiproliferative activity in BCL6-dependent DLBCL cells (IC50 = 3.2 nM). BCL6 degradation was CRBN- and proteasome-dependent and was accompanied by G1-phase arrest and increased p21 and p27 expression. Oral administration of 15 inhibited tumor growth in an OCI-LY1 xenograft model (TGI = 84% at 20 mg/kg) and reduced tumor BCL6 and Ki67 levels without appreciable body-weight loss or overt major-organ histopathology. Overall, compound 15 represents a promising BCL6 PROTAC degrader for DLBCL.

item.title: Discovery of Indazole-Based Dual-Pharmacophore Inhibitors of Dengue and Zika Proteases as Promising Antivirals
item.description:
Abstract
Flavivirus outbreaks caused by dengue virus (DENV) and Zika virus (ZIKV) remain a major global health challenge, with no FDA-approved antivirals available. Herein, we designed, synthesized, and evaluated indazole-based dual pharmacophore motifs targeting NS2B-NS3 serine proteases, essential for viral replication. Enzymatic assays revealed nanomolar to sub-micromolar potency, with strong selectivity over host serine proteases, minimizing off-target risks. Biophysical studies showed ligand-induced thermal stabilization, while kinetic and dialysis analyses confirmed a reversible, competitive, non-covalent inhibition mechanism. In DENV-infected Vero CCL-81 cells, several leads exhibited potent antiviral activity with low cytotoxicity. Notably, compound C8 demonstrated low-nanomolar enzyme inhibition against both viruses, translating to complete viral suppression in cells (EC50 = 0.5 μM) with a good selectivity index, underscoring its therapeutic potential. Molecular docking and molecular dynamics simulations supported these findings, revealing key active-site interactions consistent with potency and specificity. Collectively, these results highlight indazole-based dual-pharmacophore inhibitors as promising anti-flaviviral leads.

item.title: Lipid Droplet-Targeted Near-Infrared II Type I AIE Photosensitizer Promotes Ferroptosis by Activating Lipophagy
item.description:
Abstract
Lipophagy, a selective autophagic pathway, maintains lipid homeostasis and contributes to ferroptosis by supplying lipid peroxidation substrates. However, organic photosensitizers that activate lipophagy to promote ferroptosis remain scarce. Herein, we developed a NIR-II emissive photosensitizer (MBTTD) targeting lipid droplets (LDs). Compared with its analogue MBTTA, stronger electron-withdrawing groups bathochromically shifted absorption/emission and tuned excited-state decay, enabling efficient type I reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation and high photothermal conversion efficiency. MBTTD nanoparticles (NPs) localized to LDs upon cellular uptake. Upon 808 nm laser irradiation, MBTTD NP-mediated phototherapy disrupted LDs and induced Rab7-regulated lipophagy, releasing polyunsaturated fatty acids that underwent ROS-driven peroxidation, triggering extensive lipid peroxidation and ferroptosis. Concurrently, MBTTD-NP-mediated phototherapy triggered endoplasmic reticulum stress and apoptosis. MBTTD NPs showed favorable biocompatibility and potent therapeutic efficacy in multicellular tumor spheroids. In vivo studies revealed that MBTTD NPs enabled NIR-II imaging-guided phototherapy, suppressing 4T1 tumor growth without significant systemic toxicity.

item.title: Structure-Based Design of HDAC6 Inhibitors Targeting the L2 Pocket: Modulating Autophagy and Liquid−Liquid Phase Separation in Lung Cancer
item.description:
Abstract
We herein describe the structure-based design, synthesis and biological evaluation of a new class of histone deacetylase 6 (HDAC6) inhibitors guided by X-ray crystal structures of our previously identified compounds 13-15. X-ray co-crystal structures of second-generation inhibitors 19b (Subseries I) and 20b (Subseries II) within zHDAC6 CD2 confirmed that these compounds behave as highly potent HDAC6 inhibitors with the ability to engage the S531 residue in the L2 loop HDAC6 catalytic domain. Western-blot analysis confirmed the target engagement in cell-based settings, through the increase of acetylated tubulin levels, without significant variation in the histone acetylation status. Compound 20b extensively reduced the viability of A549 cells in both 2- and 3-dimensional cell cultures, through the activation of pro-autophagic pathways. In addition, HDAC6 inhibition impaired the nucleation of stress-granules, confirming the ability of these compounds to modulate liquid−liquid phase separation, an emerging HDAC6-driven hallmark in cancer.

item.title: Development of N -Hydroxyindole-2-Carboxamides as New Host-Targeted Broad-Spectrum Antiviral Agents Against Human Respiratory Viruses
item.description:
Abstract
Endoplasmic reticulum (ER) oxidoreductases are promising targets for host-targeted antiviral agents (HTAs) because of their essential role in protein folding, including the maturation of viral proteins. Human protein disulfide isomerase family member A3 (PDIA3) is involved in the folding of N-glycosylated client proteins, including viral envelope proteins, making it an attractive but underexplored antiviral target. Here, we describe the discovery of a novel N-hydroxyindole-2-carboxamide class of PDIA3 inhibitors, exemplified by compound AV22 (1o), which effectively inhibits PDIA3 activity and exerts broad-spectrum antiviral activity against major human respiratory viruses. Mechanistic studies indicated that AV22 (1o) increased the release of non-infectious coronavirus particles and reduced disulfide bond formation in the coronavirus spike protein, indicating that its antiviral effect stems from interference with PDIA3 activity. This new class of HTAs provides promising leads for drug discovery targeting viral envelope protein maturation vulnerabilities and is suitable for developing new BSAs.

item.title: Discovery of Novel STING Inhibitors for the Treatment of Severe Acute Pancreatitis
item.description:
Abstract
Stimulator of interferon genes (STING) is a promising therapeutic target for severe acute pancreatitis (SAP), but effective small-molecule inhibitors remain limited. Here, structure−activity relationship studies identified compound D4 as a potent STING inhibitor with favorable cellular activity and safety. D4 directly engaged STING, inhibited its oligomerization and downstream TBK1/IRF3 signaling, and restored macrophage phagocytosis, autophagic flux, and mitochondrial function while suppressing NOD-like receptor family pyrin domain containing 3(NLRP3)-associated pyroptosis. D4 showed oral exposure with 24.70% bioavailability and no overt toxicity at 1000 mg/kg. In a caerulein/LPS-induced SAP model, D4 markedly reduced pancreatic injury, acinar cell necrosis, inflammatory infiltration, and serum amylase and lipase levels. STING knockdown produced similar protective effects. These findings identify D4 as a promising STING-targeting lead compound for SAP treatment.

item.title: Cinchona Alkaloids-Derived Ammonium Salts for Long-Acting and Sensory-Selective Nerve Blockades
item.description:
Abstract
Local anesthetics (LAs), a type of substance with the ability of blocking nerve fiber conduction, are indispensable in clinical practice for pain relief. However, the duration of action and sensory-motor nerve selectivity of conventional LAs require further optimization. Herein, we wish to report the discovery of novel ammonium salts derived from natural cinchona alkaloids for long-acting and sensory-selective nerve blockades. The bicyclic quincoridine skeleton exhibited superior nerve blockade efficacy compared to acyclic and monocyclic analogs. Compound CLA-1-3 produced prolonged nerve blockade (over 50 h) in the rat sciatic nerve block model, possessing an IC50 value of approximately 0.39 μmol/L for voltage-gated sodium channel inhibition. On the other hand, at a concentration range of 0.30% to 0.60%, compound CLA-3-5 achieved sensory-selective nerve blockade lasting up to 3 h. The candidate molecules and underlying mechanistic insights will be valuable assets for drug development and therapeutic innovation.

item.title: Repurposing Approved Chemotherapeutics as Intrinsic Photosensitizers for Single-Molecule Chemophototherapy
item.description:
Abstract
Chemophototherapy (CPT), combining chemotherapy and photodynamic therapy (PDT), is a promising strategy to enhance anticancer efficacy while reducing systemic toxicity. Many approved drugs contain chromophoric moieties that absorb visible light, suggesting their potential as intrinsic photosensitizers. Herein, we introduce a single-molecule chemophototherapy (SM-CPT) approach based on computational screening of approved anticancer drugs for repurposing as photosensitizers. A curated library of 238 small-molecule drugs was screened using time-dependent density functional theory to identify compounds with favourable photophysical properties. Fifteen candidates were identified, and mitoxantrone, pixantrone, daunorubicin, and epirubicin were selected for experimental validation. All compounds generated reactive oxygen species upon irradiation and showed enhanced cytotoxicity in breast cancer cell models, with up to an order-of-magnitude reduction in half-maximal inhibitory concentration values. The approach was further validated in ovarian cancer models, including platinum-resistant cells and patient-derived ascites, highlighting SM-CPT as a translationally attractive light-activated cancer therapy.

item.title: Rational Design of Near-Infrared Difluoroboron Cyanine Photosensitizers for Lipid Droplet-Targeting Imaging and Tumor Therapy
item.description:
Abstract
Specifically disrupting lipid droplets (LDs) is an effective strategy for ablating tumor cells through photodynamic therapy (PDT). However, most reported LD probes possess short excitation/emission wavelengths, limiting tissue penetration, and LD-targeted theranostic probes remain underdeveloped. In this work, we first developed a family of near-infrared (NIR) charge-neutral and lipid droplet-targeting cyanine photosensitizers by systematically introducing heavy atoms (Br/I) at different sites of electrically neutral BF2-bridged cyanine (BCy5). These BCy photosensitizers retain the characteristic near-infrared absorption (>650 nm) and high molar extinction coefficients of classical cyanine dyes while exhibiting good singlet oxygen quantum yields. Notably, BCy5-Br1−BCy5-Br3 nanoparticles with high LD specificity exhibit significant PDT efficacy at submicromolar concentrations and, by inducing oxidative stress and lipid peroxidation (LPO) accumulation, concurrently trigger apoptosis and ferroptosis, effectively suppressing melanoma growth in vivo. This work provides vital insights into design principles and transformation of LD-targeting NIR cyanine photosensitizers for cancer PDT.

item.title: Development of DCL1191 as a Potent, Selective and Orally Bioavailable Inhibitor for Autophagy-Associated Transcription Factor EB (TFEB)
item.description:
Abstract
Transcription factor EB (TFEB) is a promising target for autophagy regulation and cancer therapy, yet it has long been regarded as an undruggable protein. Starting from eltrombopag, an FDA-approved agent that exhibits both thrombopoietin receptor (Tpo-R) agonistic activity and TFEB inhibitory potency, we performed systematic structure−activity relationship optimization and identified DCL1191 as a potent, selective, and orally bioavailable TFEB inhibitor. DCL1191 binds TFEB with a Kd of 80.5 nM and disrupts the TFEB-DNA interaction with an IC50 of 60.5 nM. Computational modeling combined with site-directed mutagenesis elucidated its precise binding mode. DCL1191 exhibits diminished activity toward Tpo-R and MITF. Mechanistically, DCL1191 effectively represses the transcription of TFEB target genes and blocks intracellular autophagic flux. In autophagy-hyperactivated U87 glioblastoma cells, DCL1191 substantially sensitizes tumor cells to temozolomide chemotherapy. Pharmacokinetic evaluation in rats further demonstrated that DCL1191 possesses an i.v. half-life of 16.33 h and satisfactory oral bioavailability of 18.77%.

item.title: Antivirulence Benzothiophenes Inhibit Intracellular Mycobacterium tuberculosis by Targeting the Sensor Histidine Kinase MprB
item.description:
Abstract
Pulmonary tuberculosis remains one of the most prevalent and threatening infectious diseases. Classical anti-tubercular therapy targets essential enzymes of the pathogen Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb), thereby suppressing bacterial growth. However, the emergence of drug-resistant strains necessitates alternative therapeutic approaches. Virulence inhibition is a promising strategy that blocks Mtb virulence factors required for survival within host cells. We previously identified a hit compound, BTP15, which protected fibroblasts and THP-1 macrophages from Mtb-induced cell death ex vivo by blocking phagosomal escape through inhibition of the mycobacterial histidine kinase MprB. Due to poor pharmacokinetics, the structure of BTP15 was optimized. New benzothiophene derivatives were screened for MprB inhibition, microsomal stability, toxicity, and ex vivo efficacy in THP-1 and MRC-5 cells. The lead compound, 7a, exhibited favorable pharmacokinetic parameters, showed no toxicity in mice at 250 mg/kg, and prevented Mtb dissemination in an acute mouse model of tuberculosis.

item.title: Developing a Ferric(III) Agent for Targeted Inhibition of Growth and Metastasis of Triple-Negative Breast Cancer Based on Human Serum Albumin by Chemodynamic Therapy-Driven Synergistic Therapy
item.description:
Abstract
Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) remains challenging due to its aggressiveness and the lack of targeted therapies. In this study, we proposed designing a ferric (Fe) agent based on human serum albumin (HSA) for chemodynamic therapy-driven synergistic therapy. To this end, we not only optimized a series of Fe(III) compounds to obtain Fe4, which has remarkable toxicity against TNBC cells, but we also constructed the HSA-Fe4 NPs delivery system. Structural analysis revealed that Fe4 binds within the IB subdomain of HSA, with His-146 coordinating the iron center. Importantly, Fe4/HSA-Fe4 NPs significantly suppressed the metastasis and growth of TNBC in vivo. Moreover, we elucidated the mechanisms by which Fe4/HSA-Fe4 NPs inhibited the growth and metastasis of TNBC: inducing Fenton reaction-mediated chemodynamic therapy, inducing ferroptosis, and tri-activating the immune response through the activation of the cGAS-STING pathway, the induction of immunogenic cell death, and the repolarization of M2 macrophages.

item.title: Discovery of Thiazolamide-based PI4KIIIβ/HDAC Dual Inhibitors with Potent Activity against Hepatitis C Virus
item.description:
Abstract
Chronic hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection remains a critical global public health burden affecting hundreds of millions of people worldwide. The emergence of antiviral resistance persistently undermines the long-term clinical efficacy of current direct-acting antiviral (DAA) regimens, creating an urgent need for therapeutics with different mechanisms of action. Host-directed multi-target therapy offers a promising avenue to overcome DAA resistance, yet dual inhibitors targeting HCV-essential host kinase phosphatidylinositol 4-kinase IIIβ (PI4KIIIβ) and epigenetic regulator histone deacetylases (HDACs) have not been reported for HCV treatment to date. Herein, we describe the rational design, chemical synthesis, and comprehensive biological evaluation of a series of novel thiazolamide-based dual PI4KIIIβ/HDAC inhibitors. Lead compounds displayed potent dual-target enzymatic inhibition, robust in vitro anti-HCV activity and excellent in vivo tolerability. This work establishes a novel host-directed dual-target therapeutic paradigm for HCV, providing a viable strategy to address the unmet clinical challenge of DAA resistance.

item.title: Discovery of a Novel Dual Inhibitor Targeting Tubulin and Histone Deacetylase 8 for Treatment of the Ovarian Cancer
item.description:
Abstract
In this work, a series of novel dual inhibitors against both tubulin and histone deacetylase (HDAC) were designed and synthesized by integrating the natural product Millepachine with the key pharmacophore of HDAC inhibitors. Among them, compound 6 exhibited potent antiproliferative activity against 12 cancer cell lines, with IC50 values ranging from 0.020 to 0.244 μM. Mechanistic investigations revealed that compound 6 inhibited both tubulin polymerization (IC50 2.0 μM) and HDAC8 (IC50 0.110 μM), with 54-, 27- and 132-fold selectivity over HDAC1, HDAC4 and HDAC6, respectively. In an ovarian cancer xenograft mouse model, compound 6 exhibited significant inhibitory effect on tumor growth with a favorable safety profile. These findings identify compound 6 as a promising tubulin/HDAC8 dual inhibitor for further investigation.

item.title: Evaluation of 68 Ga Labeling Strategies and Thermostability of HER2-Targeted Nanobody NB46
item.description:
Abstract
The HER2-targeted nanobody NB46 was evaluated for labeling strategy flexibility and thermostability. Random and site-specific 68Ga labeling strategies were compared. Both conjugates exhibited high HER2 affinity, comparable to unmodified NB46. Cellular uptake, pharmacokinetics, micro-PET/CT imaging, and biodistribution in HER2-positive and HER2-negative tumor-bearing mice revealed no significant differences between the two strategies. NB46 retained HER2 affinity at temperatures up to 90 °C, demonstrating exceptional thermostability. Both conjugates achieved >95% radiochemical yields at all tested temperatures. Micro-PET/CT imaging showed sustained high tumor uptake with renal clearance as the primary elimination pathway. Blocking studies confirmed that NB46 and trastuzumab competitively bind to HER2. Elevated labeling temperatures did not compromise tumor targeting but resulted in a mild increase in renal uptake, notably for the random conjugate at 90 °C. These findings suggest that random labeling may represent a simpler, equally effective alternative for 68Ga-NB46 preparation, and confirm the excellent thermostability of this nanobody scaffold.

item.title: Design, Synthesis and Evaluation Donepezil-Based Dual BuChE/FAAH Inhibitors for Alzheimer’s Disease Therapy
item.description:
Abstract
Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is multifactorial, prompting multi-target therapy. A series of donepezil-based derivatives were designed, synthesized, and evaluated as dual inhibitors of human butyrylcholinesterase (hBuChE) and fatty acid amide hydrolase (hFAAH). Among them, lead G15 displayed potent and balanced inhibition with IC50 values of 2.44 μM and 0.17 μM, respectively, and favorable selectivity over carboxylesterases CES1/2 (SI 14.4 and 8.4). G15 not only acted as a time-dependent, mixed-type hFAAH inhibitor and a pseudo-irreversible hBuChE inhibitor, but also exhibited good drug-like properties, including high BBB permeability and oral bioavailability (108%). Moreover, G15 chelated Zn2+, protected PC12 cells from oxidative stress, and promoted microglial M1 → M2 polarization. In an Aβ1−42-induced mouse model, G15 significantly reversed cognitive deficits, outperforming donepezil. Therefore, G15 is poised for further development as a promising multi-target candidate for AD therapy.

Enzyme−Targeted Therapeutics for Neurological Disorders
item.description:
Abstract
Neurological disorders represent one of the leading causes of disability and mortality worldwide, and their prevalence is expected to increase substantially with population aging. Despite major advances in neuroscience, effective disease-modifying therapies remain unavailable for most chronic disorders of the central nervous system (CNS), highlighting the need for novel therapeutic strategies. Enzymes are attractive drug targets because they regulate fundamental processes including neurotransmission, signal transduction, energy metabolism, protein homeostasis, epigenetic regulation, lipid metabolism, and cellular detoxification. This review summarizes the major classes of druggable CNS enzymes, discuss clinically approved drugs and emerging investigational agents, and evaluate therapeutic opportunities across neurodegenerative, neurodevelopmental, neuropsychiatric, cerebrovascular, and neuro-oncologic diseases. Key challenges including blood−brain barrier penetration, target selectivity, off-target pharmacology, and clinical translation are also examined. By integrating diverse enzyme-targeting modalities across multiple neurological disorders, this review highlights both the progress achieved to date and the substantial opportunities that remain for future CNS drug discovery.

item.title: Maleimide−Thiol Conjugation Enables the Optimization of 68 Ga-Labeled CAIX Targeting PET Probes
item.description:
Abstract
Carbonic anhydrase IX (CAIX) is a well-established biomarker of tumor hypoxia and an attractive target for molecular imaging. Despite the development of small-molecule CAIX-targeting positron emission tomography (PET) probes, most exhibit high normal-organ uptake and suboptimal tumor-to-background contrast. Moreover, their application in hypoxic tumors remains insufficiently explored. Herein, we reported four 68Ga-labeled CAIX-targeting probes based on the acetazolamide (AAZ) scaffold, employing distinct conjugation strategies, including amide coupling and maleimide−thiol ligation. All probes demonstrated detectable tumor uptake in vivo. Among them, [68Ga]Ga-SMIC-2607 displayed the highest tumor uptake (14.67 ± 3.06 %ID/g) and tumor-to-kidney ratio (1.69 ± 0.41) at 1 h in subcutaneous OS-RC-2-bearing mice, along with high tumor uptake in HT-29-bearing mice (2.98 ± 0.28 %ID/g at 1 h). Overall, [68Ga]Ga-SMIC-2607 demonstrates favorable imaging characteristics, with high tumor uptake and high tumor-to-normal organ ratios, representing a promising candidate for imaging CAIX-overexpressing tumors and supporting clinical translation.

item.title: A Peripheral Sulfonium Moiety Engineering Strategy to Enhance AIEgen-Based Antitumor Photodynamic Therapy
item.description:
Abstract
The therapeutic efficacy of photosensitizers (PSs) strongly depends on their capacity to efficiently generate reactive oxygen species (ROS). Herein, we report a peripheral sulfonium moiety engineering strategy and identify a lead aggregation-induced emission (AIE)-based PS, S12. The sulfonium moiety enhances the photosensitization of S12 primarily by increasing spin−orbit coupling (SOC) and reducing ΔEST, thus boosting ROS generation. Moreover, the sulfonium unit enables S12 to simultaneously produce both Type I and Type II ROS, rendering its photosensitization weakly dependent on O2 concentration. Owing to its cationic character and the inherent amphiphilicity of the AIE core, S12 exhibits dynamic organelle-targeting behavior, initially anchoring to membranes and subsequently accumulating in lipid droplets. Such localization facilitates ROS-triggered ferroptosis, leading to potent in vitro antitumor photodynamic therapy activity and effective tumor suppression in a 4T1 mouse model. Overall, this work provides a rational design strategy to advance AIE-based PSs with enhanced therapeutic potential.

item.title: A Selective Bis-Catecholate Siderophore-Ampicillin Conjugate Expands Activity against Multidrug-Resistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa
item.description:
Abstract
Antimicrobial resistance is a global public health crisis, with multidrug-resistant P. aeruginosa among the most critical threats. The high cost and slow pace of novel antibiotic development, coupled with rapid resistance evolution, demand innovative strategies. Here, we present a Trojan horse approach using siderophore-antibiotic conjugates (SACs) to hijack bacterial iron uptake systems and deliver β-lactam payloads across the Gram-negative outer membrane. We designed a series of ampicillin conjugates with mono-catecholate, bis-catecholate, and catecholate-hydroxamate siderophores. These conjugates demonstrate potent antimicrobial activity. Notably, the lead compound, BC-2-Amp, shows broad-spectrum and highly selective activity against a panel of 105 clinical isolates of P. aeruginosa. Mechanistic studies demonstrated that BC-2-Amp utilizes PiuA as a critical receptor for targeted delivery. Complementary in vivo experiments further confirmed its promising therapeutic efficacy. Collectively, these findings establish SACs as a potent strategy for broadening the spectrum of β-lactam antibiotics and provide a robust platform for high-potency drug delivery.

item.title: Discovery of Diaryl Pyrimidine-Guanidine Derivatives as Jumonji C Domain-Containing Lysine Histone Demethylase (KDM) Inhibitors with In Vivo Anti-Cervical Cancer Activity
item.description:
Abstract
JMJD family histone demethylases are highly expressed in cervical cancer and promote tumor progression, highlighting their potential as therapeutic targets for this malignancy. Using a scaffold-hopping-based virtual screening, we discovered a series of diaryl pyrimidine-guanidine derivatives as KDM6B inhibitors. The optimized compound 40 exhibited potent KDM6B inhibitory activity comparable to that of GSK-J4, but differs mechanistically by being non-competitive with 2-OG. Although 40 showed pan-KDM inhibition in enzymatic level, it selectively elevated H3K27me3 levels in C33A cells without affecting H3K4me3 or H3K9me3. In C33A cells, 40 suppressed proliferation, induced cell-cycle arrest and apoptosis. In a xenograft mouse model, 40 inhibited tumor growth, downregulated Ki-67, and upregulated cleaved caspase-3, p-H2A.X, and H3K27me3. Collectively, 40 represents a promising chemical probe for investigating JMJD KDMs and H3K27 modifications in cervical cancer and establishes a foundation for developing targeted agents.

item.title: Development of Potent G Protein Pathway-Biased GPR183 Agonists
item.description:
Abstract
GPR183 is an oxysterol-sensing GPCR predominantly expressed in lymphoid organs and tissues. Activation of the receptor by oxysterol 7α,25-OHC leads to Gαi protein-mediated signaling as well as β-arrestin2 recruitment. GPR183/oxysterol signaling modulates localization of lymphoid cells; consequently, the receptor is associated with several inflammation-associated diseases and is an interesting potential drug target. Previously, we reported the discovery of moderately potent G protein-biased partial agonists for GPR183 from a virtual screening based on the antagonist NIBR189. Herein, we present the detailed structure−activity investigations and optimizations, which led to the identification of full agonists for GPR183 with complete bias for G protein signaling and low nanomolar potency, including 63 (TUG-2604) with potency and efficacy similar to 7α,25-OHC. Notably, 63 was unable to induce migration of human dendritic cells but inhibited migration induced by 7α,25-OHC. This compound will be valuable for further explorations of the signaling-specific function and drug target potential of GPR183.

item.title: Design, Synthesis, and Pharmacological Profiling of Serine/Threonine Kinase 33 (STK33) Inhibitors for Nonhormonal Male Contraception
item.description:
Abstract
Serine/threonine kinase 33 (STK33) is a male germ-specific nonhormonal contraceptive target that is both genetically and chemically validated. Building on our previously reported reversible male contraceptive inhibitor, CDD-2807, we conducted systematic structure−activity relationship (SAR) and structure−property relationship (SPR) studies on the 3-(biphenylethynyl)-1H-indazole scaffold to address key drug development liabilities, most notably poor kinetic solubility. These efforts identified CDD-3094, which exhibits a balanced profile characterized by retained nanomolar cellular potency, >100 μM kinetic solubility, comparable metabolic stability, reduced human ether-à-go-go-related gene (hERG) channel inhibition, and a favorable cellular kinase profile, with 278 of 300 kinases (92.7%) displaying <30% occupancy at 1000 nM. Leveraging X-ray crystallography of the STK33/CDD-3094 complex, we performed structure-based modifications to specifically target the primary off-target liability, CDC-like kinase 4 (CLK4). This work culminated in the discovery of compound 40, which achieved 446-fold biochemical selectivity for STK33 over CLK4. While its cellular potency is attenuated to >1 μM, this analog provides a valuable biochemical tool for investigating STK33 selectivity and highlights the challenges of balancing kinase discrimination with intracellular activity. Collectively, these studies establish a foundation for developing soluble STK33 inhibitors, facilitating further preclinical refinement of nonhormonal male contraceptives.

item.title: Development of Next-Generation ALDH1B1 Inhibitors with Enhanced Pharmacological and Functional Properties
item.description:
Abstract
ALDH1B1 is a mitochondrial aldehyde dehydrogenase required for the survival of stem-like colorectal and pancreatic cancer cells. Isoform-selective guanidinyl antagonists of aldehyde dehydrogenases (IGUANAs) have been developed for ALDH1B1, and here we describe structure−activity relationship (SAR) studies of three scaffold components: the bicyclic guanidine core, a substituted aryl ring that engages the catalytic site, and a biaryl group that interacts with flanking residues. We further show that previously reported IGUANAs are metabolically labile and rapidly effluxed from intestinal epithelial cells. To address these limitations, we have explored bioisosteres of the biaryl moiety and modifications of the guanidine core. These investigations have yielded the aryl-alkyl ether derivative IGUANA-5, a potent ALDH1B1 inhibitor that selectively blocks the growth of colon and pancreatic cancer spheroids and exhibits enhanced in vitro and in vivo pharmacological properties. Our findings establish a new class of ALDH1B1 inhibitors that could inform the advancement of anti-cancer therapies.

item.title: Simplification and Derivatization of Quinoline-Containing M41 Lead to the Discovery of NADPH Oxidase Isoform-Selective Inhibitors Effective in Cancer Cells
item.description:
Abstract
NADPH oxidases (NOXs) are attractive but challenging drug targets. Starting from M41 and its analog MC4876, we synthesized quinoline-based derivatives. SAR studies revealed that modifications at the quinoline C2 position and the amine-moiety influenced potency and isoform preference. Boc-protected analogs preferred NOX5, (compound 1a: IC50 = 1.6 μM), whereas deprotected derivatives favored NOX2. Replacing piperidine with tetrahydropyran afforded 1e, a selective NOX1 inhibitor (IC50 = 3.4 μM). The bisquinoline derivative 2a emerged as the most potent, selective NOX2 inhibitor (IC50 = 1.4 μM; cellular EC50 = 0.89 μM). Computational studies support binding at the NADPH site and attribute 2a′s enhanced potency to additional interactions. MC4876 displayed antiproliferative activity, reducing glioblastoma cell viability, glucose uptake, HK2 expression, and mesenchymal markers, while lowering ROS and inducing mitochondrial dysfunction and DNA damage in U937 cells. These findings identify quinoline as tunable scaffolds for isoform-selective NOX inhibition, with 1e and 2a as promising leads.

item.title: Beyond Inhibition: Targeted Degradation of NLRP3 by Autophagy-Tethering Bifunctional Compounds as a Therapy for Inflammatory Bowel Disease
item.description:
Abstract
Based on our previous finding that the NLRP3 inhibitor LD5 dually binds LC3 and NLRP3, we elucidated the key functional groups responsible for its engagement with NLRP3. Leveraging this insight, we designed and synthesized a library of bivalent LD5-based autophagy-targeting chimeras (ATTECs), from which M3 emerged as the most potent NLRP3 degrader. We further sought to rationalize this approach by investigating the fundamental pharmacological questions: why develop a degrader from an existing inhibitor and what advantages would such a degrader offer over the inhibitor? Comparative studies in a colitis model clearly established that the degrader M3 achieves sustained anti-inflammatory efficacy, both in vitro and in vivo, outperforming its inhibitor precursor LD5. Our study extends beyond the discovery of a potential degrader for inflammatory bowel disease to demonstrate the crucial long-lasting therapeutic advantage of degraders over inhibitors in treating this condition.

item.title: Deciphering the Structure−Activity Relationships Underpinning the Linkerology of Bivalent EGFR Inhibitors
item.description:
Abstract
Linking small molecules that bind adjacent sites on a target is a promising strategy for developing compounds with tight binding affinities. ATP-allosteric bivalent inhibitors (AABIs) of the epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) have provided new insights into efficient linker design where large potency gains can be achieved through particular design scenarios. In this work, we systematically evaluated the structure−activity relationships of target molecules to better understand the most effective approach to maximizing potency through linker optimization. Our results show that linker length and points of connection are both important strategies for significant potency enhancements. Structures and simulations indicate that maximal flexibility is likely the most important design criterion for linking molecules that occupy adjacent pockets, as modeled by the EGFR kinase domain. These studies provide a general framework for the rational design of linkers broadly relevant to fragment-based drug discovery and a number of related scenarios in medicinal chemistry.

item.title: [Graphical abstract added] Design and Development of New Dual Target Agents, Cannabinoid Subtype 2 Receptor (CB2R) Agonists, and Fatty Acid Amide Hydrolase (FAAH) Inhibitors against Neurodegeneration
Chimeric Hsp90β-Selective Inhibitors Confer Enhanced Affinity, Selectivity, and Drug-Like Properties
item.description:
Abstract
The clinical evaluation of 90 kD heat shock protein (Hsp90) inhibitors has been hindered by their detrimental, pan-inhibitory activities. Consequently, the development of Hsp90 isoform-selective inhibitors has been pursued. Although prior compounds have elucidated the roles of Hsp90β in cancer immunotherapy and opioid therapy, their sub-optimal drug-like properties have required extensive optimization campaigns to enhance this scaffold’s pharmacological profile. The work presented herein expands upon previous efforts by introducing simultaneous modifications to the “northern” indazolone fragment and “southwestern” appendage to determine whether combinations of the properties at these regions can produce improved Hsp90β-selective inhibitors. These chimeric inhibitors reveal that such modifications can retain Hsp90β affinity/selectivity, while modulating key pharmacokinetic parameters and anticancer activity. Notably, one derivative (8b) also exhibits oral bioavailability and enhances opioid antinociception in a murine model for chronic pain. These findings support the continued development of Hsp90β-selective inhibitors for anticancer therapy, chronic pain management, and other disease indications.

item.title: Translational Application of the Five-Star Matrix for the Structure-Guided Optimization of a Bicyclopiperazine DEL Hit into Bcpz 1.5: A Potent Monoacylglycerol Lipase Inhibitor with Functional Inhibition in Human Brain Homogenate and Efficacy in Neuroinflammatory Models
item.description:
Abstract
Monoacylglycerol lipase (MAGL) is a promising therapeutic target for neuroinflammatory conditions. We have previously reported on MAGLi 432, a reversible MAGL inhibitor with activity in mouse models of neuroinflammation. In this full account, we report on the structure-guided optimization of a bicyclopiperazine (Bcpz) DEL hit into potent, selective and brain-penetrant reversible MAGL inhibitor 1.5 (MAGLi 432), guided by the “Five-Star Matrix” translational framework. Compound 1.5 combines excellent MAGL potency (IC50 = 3.2 nM) and selectivity over other serine hydrolases with favorable pharmacokinetic properties, including a 5.7 h half-life after oral administration in male Wistar rats, and CNS drug-like potential. Furthermore, as previously reported, the compound demonstrated robust brain penetration and efficacy in preclinical mouse models of neuroinflammation correlating with inhibition of MAGL activity in mouse and human brain homogenate. This work highlights the power of combining DEL screening and SBDD with the Five-Star Matrix to deliver drug-like candidates for neuroinflammatory disorders.

item.title: High-Affinity Y 1 Receptor Theranostics: First-in-Class Stabilized Nonapeptides for Breast Cancer Imaging and Therapy
item.description:
Abstract
Theranostic agents integrate diagnostic and therapeutic capabilities into a single molecular platform, offering an advanced approach to personalized medicine. The neuropeptide Y1 receptor (Y1R) is a promising target for breast cancer theranostics given its overexpression across multiple disease stages. Building on the Y1R-selective antagonist [Lys2, Arg4]BVD-15, we report the systematic development of stabilized nonapeptide analogues through strategic modifications. Lead candidates were radiolabeled in >95% radiochemical purity and showed Y1R binding affinities up to 60-fold higher than the parent peptide, no detectable plasma degradation over 90 min, and half-lives of 42−55 min in liver and kidney homogenates. PET-CT imaging in HEK-Y1R and MCF-7 tumor models demonstrated selective tumor uptake, peaking at 19.2% ID/g in HEK-Y1R tumors, with biodistribution studies confirming specific tumor accumulation and progressive clearance over 48 h. Therapeutic evaluation of lead candidate [177Lu]Lu-31 in HEK-Y1R tumor-bearing mice showed dose-dependent tumor growth inhibition, supporting this peptide class as Y1R-targeted radionuclide therapeutics.

item.title: Insights into HIF Prolyl Hydroxylase Inhibitors: Recent Advances and Expanding Therapeutic Applications beyond Anemia
item.description:
Abstract
Oxygen homeostasis is fundamental to cellular and organismal physiology and is primarily governed by the hypoxia-inducible factor (HIF) signaling pathway. Within this pathway, prolyl hydroxylase domain enzymes (PHDs) serve as a key oxygen sensor that regulates HIF-α stability and thus controls hypoxic transcriptional responses. Dysregulation of this system is implicated in a broad spectrum of hypoxia-related diseases, making PHDs an important class of therapeutic targets. This perspective summarizes recent advances in PHD inhibitors, with emphasis on structural and functional differences among PHD isoforms and the predominance of PHD2 in drug discovery. We review key screening and design strategies for both carboxylate and non-carboxylate chemotypes. Current clinical progress and major challenges, such as isoform selectivity, safety concerns, and pharmacokinetic limitations, are discussed. Finally, we highlight emerging therapeutic opportunities beyond anemia, including ischemic, metabolic, and inflammatory diseases, providing a framework for precision targeting of oxygen-sensing pathways.

item.title: Design, Synthesis, and Preliminary Investigation on the Mode of Action for a Series of Novel Antimicrobial Peptidomimetics
item.description:
Abstract
Over the years, many antibiotics have been developed, but most have become less effective due to antimicrobial resistance, especially those targeting enzymatic pathways. This growing resistance poses a serious global health threat. It is now recognized that physically disrupting bacterial cell membranes is less prone to resistance development. Antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) are promising in this regard, though their broader application is limited by their susceptibility to proteolytic degradation and toxicity. To address these issues, peptidomimetics have emerged as a new class of antibacterial agents. In this study, a library of AMPs were designed and synthesized, inspired by magainin, a defensin-mimetic molecule, and brilacidin. Modifying side chain lengths proved essential for effective insertion into phospholipid bilayers. A modular synthetic approach was developed, enabling the generation of diverse derivatives to explore structure−activity relationships. The compounds were tested against clinically relevant pathogens, showing promising antimicrobial activity, and preliminary studies confirmed a membranolytic mechanism of action.

item.title: CYP1B1 Enzymatic Activity Promotes Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer Metastasis: Antimetastatic Effects of Novel CYP1B1 Inhibitors
item.description:
Abstract
Metastasis represents a major cause of chemotherapy failure in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). To explore the role of CYP1B1 enzymatic activity in NSCLC metastasis, we established A549 and H460 cells overexpressing wild-type CYP1B1, an activity-enhanced variant (L432V), and an activity-reduced variant (N203S). CYP1B1 did not affect cell proliferation but promoted migration and invasion, with the extent of these effects being associated with CYP1B1 enzymatic activity. We then designed and synthesized a series of CYP1B1 inhibitors. Compound G26 exhibited high selectivity over other CYP isoforms (IC50 = 5.33 nM), showed favorable microsomal metabolic stability with species differences, significantly inhibited migration and invasion in A549 and H460 cells, exhibited moderate oral bioavailability in SD rats (F = 20.7%), and showed a favorable safety profile in mice.

item.title: Krüppel-like Factors in Autophagy: A Spatiotemporal Rheostat Framework Linking Cellular Fate and Disease
item.description:
Abstract
Macroautophagy/autophagy links environmental cues to cellular adaptation, differentiation, and pathology. Krüppel-like factors (KLFs) influence autophagy across diverse contexts, yet their effects differ in direction and biological outcome, challenging a simple activation-versus-inhibition model. This perspective proposes a spatiotemporal rheostat framework for organizing KLF-autophagy interactions across cell-fate and disease contexts. It defines four experimentally testable dimensionsgraded modulation, temporal dependence, stage specificity, and reversibilityand evaluates representative studies using flux-aware evidence grading. Current evidence most strongly supports context- and stage-dependent KLF regulation, particularly through transcriptional control of early and intermediate autophagy components, whereas graded responses, temporal dynamics, and reversibility remain priorities for direct testing. Pharmacological analysis indicates that reported strategies rely mainly on upstream, pathway-level, or transcript-directed modulation, whereas direct KLF protein engagement remains unestablished. By reconciling heterogeneous evidence, the framework enables cross-context comparison and provides a basis for future mechanism-guided therapeutic investigation of the KLF-autophagy axis.

item.title: Discovery of Potent, Selective DNMT1 PROTAC Degraders: Simultaneous Blockade of Catalytic and Non-Catalytic Functions for Liver Fibrosis Therapy
item.description:
Abstract
Liver fibrosis is a progressive pathological condition driven by chronic hepatic injury and currently lacks effective therapies. DNA methyltransferase 1 (DNMT1) promotes fibrogenesis through both catalytic and non-catalytic mechanisms. To simultaneously target these dual functions, we designed and synthesized a series of DNMT1-targeting PROTAC degraders based on DC-517. Our optimization campaign culminated in compound B7, which emerged as the most potent agent, mediating ubiquitin-proteasomal degradation of DNMT1. In vitro, B7 reduced global DNA methylation and altered readouts associated with reported catalytic and non-catalytic functions of DNMT1, concomitant with suppression of profibrotic responses. In vivo, B7 administration reduced DNMT1 expression and attenuated liver fibrosis, as evidenced by decreased collagen deposition and improved hepatic function. Overall, these findings indicate that DNMT1 degradation could be a viable approach for liver fibrosis and provide a proof of concept for applying PROTAC technology to fibrotic diseases.

item.title: Discovery of an HDAC2-Selective Inhibitor via Enzyme−Inhibitor-Binding Thermodynamics/Kinetics as a Prospective Neurological Disorder Drug
item.description:
Abstract
In this study, we identified KTT-1 (12) as an HDAC2-selective inhibitor through in vitro evaluations based on both thermodynamics and kinetics of the enzyme−inhibitor binding. This approach stands in sharp contrast to conventional drug discovery research, which usually focuses only on thermodynamics. An X-ray crystallography study on HDAC2 complexed with 12 in combination with quantum chemical calculations on model compounds suggested that the 2-furanyl group of 12 contributes to the selective HDAC2 inhibition. In our cellular assays, 12 preferentially inhibited HDAC2 over its highly homologous HDAC1 and promoted neurite outgrowth of neuro-2a cells. Furthermore, treatment of mice with 12 improved the memory and depression-like behavior of stress-vulnerable mice. The results indicate that 12 is a promising lead compound for neurological disorders such as Alzheimer’s disease and depression and demonstrate that inhibitor evaluations that combine enzyme−inhibitor-binding thermodynamics and kinetics are useful tools for drug discovery research.

item.title: Discovery and Optimization of a Novel Brain-Penetrant Colchicine-Binding Site Ligand for Treatment of Glioma
item.description:
Abstract
The limited number of approved drugs for treatment of brain cancers is very apparent. Temozolomide and Vorasidenib continue to be the only approved brain-permeable, orally available drugs. A novel class of highly brain-penetrant tubulin-binding ligands was discovered through rigorous structure−activity-relationship (SAR) studies. The lead compounds were validated through tubulin polymerization assays and co-crystallization, demonstrating destabilization of microtubules by binding to the colchicine site of tubulin. The ligands maintain core interactions with tubulin like those of colchicine; however, both the tubulin βT7 and αT5 loops adopt flipped conformations compared with the colchicine-bound state. SAR studies revealed high selectivity for substitutions, with a small number of indispensable moieties, and led to the selection of small-molecule compound 40 as the clinical candidate. Compound 40 is highly potent, has high gut and moderate brain permeability, a favorable clearance and cytochrome P450 inhibition/induction profile, and demonstrated activity in models of glioma.

item.title: Development of pH-Resilient Boronic Acid ENPP1 Inhibitors for STING-Mediated Cancer Immunotherapy
item.description:
Abstract
Ectonucleotide pyrophosphatase/phosphodiesterase 1 (ENPP1) hydrolyzes cGAMP within the tumor microenvironment (TME), suppressing stimulator of interferon genes (STING)-mediated antitumor immunity. Inspired by the phosphate-based inhibitor STF-1084, we developed a novel class of non-nucleotide ENPP1 inhibitors featuring a boronic acid zinc-binding group (ZBG), which led to the identification of the potent and pH-resilient compound 36. In vitro evaluations confirmed that compound 36 enhances cGAMP-mediated STING activation, driving the upregulation of key immune effectors and chemokines. Furthermore, in a syngeneic CT26 tumor model, monotherapy with compound 36 (20 mg/kg, IP) achieved a tumor growth inhibition (TGI) of 57.4%. Notably, combination therapy with a single dose of oxaliplatin (OX) exhibited a synergistic antitumor effect (TGI = 80.7%) without observable toxicity. Collectively, this study identifies compound 36 as a promising lead ENPP1 inhibitor and further highlights boronic acid as an effective ZBG for the development of ENPP1-targeted cancer immunotherapies.

item.title: [ 18 F]ApaScan: A 2-Pyridinylbenzimidazole PET Tracer with Highly Selective Binding to Human Aldosterone-Producing Adenoma Tissue
item.description:
Abstract
Aldosterone synthase (CYP11B2) is overexpressed in aldosterone-producing adenomas (APAs) and represents a promising PET target for the noninvasive localization of APA lesions in primary aldosteronism. To address this need, we synthesized and evaluated 2-pyridinylbenzimidazole analogues for their ability to bind to human APA (hAPA) tissue. Based on initial binding assays, five analogues were selected and radiolabeled with fluorine-18 for autoradiographic and saturation binding studies. Among them, [18F]3 ([18F]ApaScan) exhibited high-affinity binding to hAPA homogenates (KD = 8.4 nM) with no measurable specific binding to normal adrenal (hNA) homogenates, demonstrating excellent tissue selectivity for hAPA over hNA. Quantitative autoradiography using [18F]3 further confirmed a high hAPA-to-hNA tissue binding ratio of 18. In normal rats, [18F]3 displayed rapid adrenal uptake, efficient clearance without prolonged retention, and no skeletal accumulation. Taken together, these results suggest that [18F]3 has the potential to be developed into a PET tracer for localizing APAs in primary aldosteronism.

item.title: Design and Development of New Dual Target Agents, Cannabinoid Subtype 2 Receptor (CB2R) Agonists, and Fatty Acid Amide Hydrolase (FAAH) Inhibitors against Neurodegeneration
item.description:
Abstract
As dual modulators of Cannabinoid subtype 2 receptor (CB2R) and fatty acid amide hydrolase (FAAH)an arising therapeutic strategy against diseases based on neuroinflammationwe developed a new series of N-adamantyl-benzamides bearing an anthranilic or salicylic scaffold. Derivatives 18, 22, and 25 emerged as an interesting compromise in terms of CB2R activity, CB2R/CB1R selectivity, and FAAH inhibition. All compounds were potent FAAH inhibitors; 18 and 25 acted as unbiased CB2R agonists with no CB1R affinity, whereas 22 was a CB2R antagonist in the cAMP pathway and partial agonist in β-arrestin-2 recruitment. The three compounds were tested in monocytes and macrophages in resting and activated states and in a human activated microglia model with a potent anti-inflammatory action. These results support the CB2R and FAAH engagement as a promising dual strategy against neuroinflammation providing valuable chemical tools for probing the structural determinants underlying CB2R binding, long residence time, and biased signaling.

item.title: How Many Crystal Structures Do You Need to Trust Your Docking Results?
item.description:
Abstract
Structure-based drug discovery relies on the prediction of protein-bound poses of new molecule designs, the accuracy of which can impact downstream prioritization. While it is expected that crystal structures of similar molecules would provide the best template for predicting the poses of new designs, the time and cost required motivates identifying a point of diminishing returns for collecting new structures. Using 403 crystal structures of SARS-CoV-2 main protease from the open science COVID Moonshot project, we explore the tradeoff between the cost and utility of obtaining crystal structures for accurately predicting poses of designed molecules. We observe that similar reference ligands enable superior pose prediction and show that success plateaus after approximately five crystal structures per generic Bemis-Murcko scaffold, exceeding 95% for the campaign’s lead series. This work provides practical recommendations for resource allocation in structure-enabled drug discovery campaigns.

item.title: Discovery of a Novel Series of Benzimidazoles/Purines as Potent, Selective and Orally Active Inhibitors of the DNA Polymerase Activity of POLQ
item.description:
Abstract
DNA polymerase θ (Polθ, gene POLQ) is a key enzyme in the microhomology-mediated end joining (MMEJ) pathway to repair DNA double strand breaks (DSB). Here we report the discovery of novel, potent, selective and orally active inhibitors of the DNA polymerase activity of POLQ. Starting from a weak inhibitor of POLQ (compound 1, IC50 0.8 μM, biochemical assay), further optimization of the series led to compound 37, a potent inhibitor of POLQ (IC50 < 0.003 μM, biochemical assay), which suppressed the cellular MMEJ pathway activity (IC50 0.10 μM), showed anti-proliferative activity in homologous recombination repair (HRR) deficient cell lines (e.g. BRCA2−/− DLD-1 IC50 0.058 μM), and enhanced antiproliferative activity of the PARP 1/2 inhibitor olaparib in multiple HRR defective cell lines, with no activity in HRR proficient settings. Compound 37 showed tumor regression in the BRCA2−/− DLD-1 murine xenograft model after chronic oral dosing in combination with olaparib.

item.title: Discovery and Optimization of Isoform Selective ULK1 Degraders to Enhance Antitumor Activity in KRAS-Mutant Cancer
item.description:
Abstract
Selective targeting of ULK1 represents a promising approach to overcome autophagy-mediated resistance in KRAS-driven cancers. However, achieving selectivity over the closely related ULK2 isoform with ATP-competitive inhibitors remains challenging due to the high sequence homology within their kinase domains. Here, we describe the design, synthesis, and structure−degradation relationship studies of two cereblon-recruiting ULK1 degraders, MR-9034 and MR-9036. Structure-guided optimization led to the discovery of MR-9036 as a potent and selective ULK1 PROTAC that degrades ULK1 without affecting ULK2 or IMiD neo-substrates. Cellular and biophysical studies confirm ternary complex formation and proteasome-dependent degradation. Compared with the clinical ULK1/2 inhibitor DCC-3116, MR-9036 produces sustained autophagy suppression following compound washout. In KRASG12C-mutant NSCLC models, ULK1 degradation enhances the antiproliferative activity of sotorasib. Pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic (PK/PD) studies in mice support in vivo feasibility. These findings establish selective ULK1 degradation as a chemical strategy to interrogate ULK1 biology and enhance therapeutic response in KRAS-driven cancers.

item.title: SMILES-Based Deep Learning Enables Discovery of Chemically Modified Ultrashort Antimicrobial Peptides
item.description:
Abstract
Sequence-based models for antimicrobial peptides are limited in representing chemically modified peptides, restricting computational discovery to canonical amino acids. Here, we developed SMAMP, a SMILES-based graph deep learning framework that encodes peptides as molecular graphs and captures noncanonical residues and chemical modifications. SMAMP accurately predicted Escherichia coli MIC (MSE = 0.558, R2 = 0.542, PCC = 0.741), outperforming another SMILES-based baseline. Guided by SMAMP, we designed 19 ultrashort peptides incorporating terminal modifications or noncanonical amino acids, 13 of which exhibited antibacterial activity. Predicted MICs correlated with experimental measurements (r = 0.764). Lead peptides HP-1 and HP-2 showed potent bactericidal activity, low mammalian cytotoxicity, and reduced resistance development compared with conventional antibiotics. Both peptides protected Galleria mellonella from infection and promoted wound healing in mice. Proteomic and mechanistic analyses revealed membrane disruption coupled with oxidative stress. SMAMP provides a chemically informed strategy for discovery and optimization of modified antimicrobial peptides.

item.title: Discovery of a Protein Kinase R-like Endoplasmic Reticulum Kinase (PERK) Inhibitor Suitable for Clinical Progression
item.description:
Abstract
Protein kinase R-like endoplasmic reticulum kinase (PERK) is a key sensor in the integrated stress response (ISR) and the unfolded protein response (UPR), playing a critical role in tumor cell survival under stress conditions. Based on literature data, we identified the novel PERK inhibitor 17, of moderate potency but promising kinase selectivity and in vivo pharmacokinetics. A lead optimisation campaign focussing on careful control of lipophilicity (log D) and lipophilic ligand efficiency (LLE) led to the identification of 49 (APL-11056), a potent and selective PERK inhibitor. High permeability contributes to its excellent in vivo pharmacokinetics and can be linked to the presence of a fluorine alpha to the core benzamide, which limits recognition by efflux transporters.

item.title: Sulfonium Modification of Echinocandins: An Effective Strategy to Combat Intrinsically Resistant Cryptococcus via Membrane Disruption and Enhanced Cell Wall Biosynthesis Inhibition
item.description:
Abstract
Fungal infections claim millions of lives annually and intrinsic resistance of Cryptococcus against echinocandins severely impedes clinical treatment. In this study, sulfonium covalent modification was performed based on natural pneumocandin B0 scaffold. The obtained derivatives exhibited potent activity against Candida species and reversed innate resistance of Cryptococcus neoformans, with MIC values reaching as low as 2 μg/mL. Structural modification elevated fungal membrane permeability and induced membrane depolarization, while enhancing the inhibitory effect on glucan synthase and disturbing cell wall biosynthesis. Compounds 3h and 5h possessed low drug resistance potential, favorable safety profiles, satisfactory pharmacokinetic properties and robust in vivo antifungal efficacy. This modification strategy facilitates the development of novel antifungal candidates.

item.title: Integrated Computational Design and Experimental Approach for the Discovery of Novel Steroidal 5α-Reductase Inhibitors for Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia
item.description:
Abstract
Advancements in computational drug design have enabled rapid identification of lead molecules with improved precision and reduced experimental attrition. In this study, an integrated in silico−in vitro approach was employed to design steroidal inhibitors targeting 5α-reductase type 2 (5-AR2), a key enzyme involved in benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH). A ligand-based pharmacophore model (ADHHHR_1), developed from known inhibitors, guided the design of androstane derivatives. Subsequent 3D-QSAR and molecular docking against 5-AR2 (PDB ID: 7BW1) identified NDPR-2 and NDPR-5 as promising candidates with favorable binding interactions. Molecular dynamics simulation analysis supported the stability of ligand−protein complexes. In silico ADME predictions indicated good drug likeness and oral bioavailability. In vitro studies demonstrated low cytotoxicity in LNCaP cells and measurable inhibitory activity against 5-AR. Overall, NDPR-2 and NDPR-5 emerged as promising lead candidates for further optimization toward safer and more effective BPH therapeutics.

item.title: K i Revisited: Principles, Pitfalls, and Best Practices for Measuring Enzyme Inhibitor Affinity
Frespaciguat ( MK-5475 ): A Novel Inhaled Soluble Guanylate Cyclase Stimulator for Pulmonary Hypertension Associated with COPD
item.description:
Abstract
Soluble guanylate cyclase (sGC) stimulators are a validated therapeutic approach for pulmonary vasodilation; however, oral agents can cause systemic hypotension and may worsen ventilation-perfusion mismatch in pulmonary hypertension associated with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (PH-COPD). To address these limitations, we applied a property-driven medicinal chemistry strategy to develop an inhaled sGC stimulator that maximizes pulmonary exposure while minimizing systemic exposure. Structure−activity relationship and pharmacokinetic studies identified high systemic clearance and low permeability as key determinants of pulmonary selectivity. These insights led to the discovery of compound 15 (frespaciguat, MK-5475), a subnanomolar sGC stimulator with a prolonged target residence time and >200-fold unbound lung-to-plasma exposure following inhalation. In a rat chronic hypoxia-induced PH model, frespaciguat produced dose-dependent reductions in pulmonary arterial pressure with minimal systemic hemodynamic effects and pharmacodynamic activity persisting >24 h after a single dose. These findings and early clinical data support the development of frespaciguat as an inhaled pulmonary-selective sGC stimulator for PH-COPD.

item.title: Discovery of a BBB-Penetrant Lanosterol Derivative as an Aβ Aggregation Inhibitor for Alzheimer’s Disease
item.description:
Abstract
The abnormal aggregation of amyloid-beta (Aβ) peptides is a core driver of Alzheimer’s disease (AD). Developing central nervous system (CNS)-penetrant small-molecule Aβ inhibitors offers a complementary strategy to overcome the high costs and severe side effects of antibodies. Lanosterol has demonstrated excellent potential in inhibiting abnormal protein aggregation. However, poor physicochemical and pharmacokinetic profiles strictly hinder its direct therapeutic application. Herein, rational modifications on lanosterol were conducted to modulate the hydrophilic−lipophilic balance around the 3-hydroxyl group and aliphatic side chain. This systematic screening led to compound 10, a highly active candidate with significantly improved metabolic stability and physicochemical properties. Furthermore, oral administration of 10 rescued cognitive memory deficits and reduced the Aβ burden in the AD mouse model. This work provides a promising, CNS-active candidate for AD intervention, demonstrating that rational structural optimization of bioactive substances is a valuable strategy in the discovery of novel therapeutics for CNS diseases.

item.title: Correction to “Potent, Selective, and Brain Penetrant Ether-Linked 2-Aminopyridine Inhibitors of Human Neuronal Nitric Oxide Synthase with Excellent Oral Bioavailability”
